Raisins
rā'zənz
n. pl. (dried grapes in clusters; carried in Abigail's peace offering and given to a dying Egyptian in the field)
Old French raisin, a grape, from Latin racemus, a cluster. The Hebrew tsimmuqim means dried or shrivelled grapes, always counted in clusters and always part of a provision carried on the road.

Biblical Definition

Twice the word appears, and both scenes are about food given at the right moment. Abigail: “Then Abigail made haste, and took two hundred loaves, and two bottles of wine, and five sheep ready dressed, and five measures of parched corn, and an hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on asses” (1Sa 25:18). Her husband Nabal — a man the chapter calls churlish and evil in his doings (1Sa 25:3) — had refused David's men bread and water; his wife loaded a provision train, went down the covert of the hill, and stopped a massacre. David's answer is the verdict of heaven on her errand: “Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me” (1Sa 25:32). The other scene is in the Amalekite pursuit: David's men find a collapsed Egyptian slave in a field, give him bread and water (1Sa 30:11), and then “they gave him a piece of a cake of figs, and two clusters of raisins: and when he had eaten, his spirit came again to him: for he had eaten no bread, nor drunk any water, three days and three nights” (1Sa 30:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a raisin as a dried grape, cured either on the vine or by artificial heat, and used both as food and in medicine.

expand to see more

RAISIN, n. s as z. [Fr. raisin, a grape; L. racemus.] A dried grape.

Grapes are suffered to remain on the vine till they are perfectly ripe, and then dried in the sun or by the heat of an oven.

An hundred clusters of raisins. 1 Sam. xxv.

Raisins are used in cookery and in medicine.

Key Scripture

1Sa 25:18 — "Then Abigail made haste, and took two hundred loaves, and two bottles of wine, and five sheep ready dressed, and five measures of parched corn, and an hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on asses."

1Sa 25:3 — "Now the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail: and she was a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance: but the man was churlish and evil in his doings; and he was of the house of Caleb."

1Sa 30:12 — "And they gave him a piece of a cake of figs, and two clusters of raisins: and when he had eaten, his spirit came again to him: for he had eaten no bread, nor drunk any water, three days and three nights."

1Sa 25:32 — "And David said to Abigail, Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me:"

Modern Corruption

Abigail is claimed for two opposite programmes — as a warrant for a wife to act against her husband, and as an embarrassment to be explained away — while the text commends her wisdom and never dissolves the marriage.

expand to see more

The chapter is unusually careful about Abigail and it will not fund either party that uses her. She is called a woman of good understanding; her husband is called churlish and evil in his doings; she acts without telling him, and she prevents a slaughter. That is commended in the plainest terms by David, who blesses God for sending her and blesses her advice for keeping him from avenging himself with his own hand. So the passage does establish that a wife's submission is not a mandate to assist evil or to stand by while blood is shed, and Scripture never asks a wife to sin. What the passage does not do is dissolve the household or celebrate independence. Abigail returns home, finds Nabal drunk at a feast like a king, waits until morning, and tells him — and it is God, not she, who smites him ten days later. She acts to save life and then goes back to a marriage she did not leave.

The Egyptian in the field is a smaller story with a longer reach. He was a slave whose own master had abandoned him sick, three days without food or water, left to die in open country. David's men found him, fed him, gave him water, then figs and two clusters of raisins — and his spirit came again to him. Only afterwards does the account mention that he could lead them to the raiding party. The order is the point: bread first, and the intelligence follows as a gift rather than as the price. Where a ministry of mercy is undertaken only as a lever for something else, the Egyptian in this chapter is the standing rebuke; and where mercy is shown for its own sake, God has a way of adding what no strategy could have bought.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsimmuqim (H6778), clusters of dried grapes; with debelah (H1690), a cake of pressed figs, and nabal (H5036), foolish — the meaning of a husband's name.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsimmuqim (H6778) — raisins, dried grape clusters; Abigail's hundred clusters, and the Egyptian's two; 1 Samuel 25:18, 1 Samuel 30:12.

Hebrew debelah (H1690) — a cake of pressed figs; carried with the raisins in both scenes; 1 Samuel 30:12.

Hebrew nabal (H5036) — foolish, vile; the man's name, and the wife's own account of him; 1 Samuel 25:25.

Hebrew sekel tob — good understanding; the phrase used of Abigail; 1 Samuel 25:3.

Hebrew shub ruach — his spirit came again; the effect of food on a man three days without it; 1 Samuel 30:12.

Usage

"“An hundred clusters of raisins” — a provision train that stopped a massacre."

"“When he had eaten, his spirit came again to him” — a slave left to die, and fed first."

"“Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me” — heaven's verdict on the errand."
